newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: BIS Shrapnel sees strong Australian housing demand.
newsitem.headline: BIS Shrapnel sees strong Australian housing demand.

text.p: For the first time since 1992 demand for housing in Australia is exceeding new construction, Australian property consultants BIS Shrapnel said on Monday.
"Stock surpluses are declining and underlying demand is increasing, setting the scene for a buoyant medium term outlook for the residential construction industry," the consultant said.
BIS Shrapnel director of building services, Rober Mellor, said he was forecasting an increase in dwelling commencements of 13 percent in 1997/98 to June 30 with recovery in all states.

Mellor said he expected underlying demand to increase three percent to 137,400 dwellings a year to 2001/02, driven by higher net overseas migration projected around the turn of the century, and by stronger population growth in the 30-34 and the 45-plus age groups, compared with the past five years.
BIS Shrapnel forecasts dwelling commencements of 123,150 for the current financial year.
It said the figure was about eight percent below the average annual level of underlying demand for the past six years and 10 percent below expected underlying demand.
"However, inroads have still to be made into the significant excess supply that built up over the three years to June 1996," the consultant said.
"BIS Shrapnel estimates that at June 1995 this surplus numbered 66,000 dwellings across Australia and triggered the major downturn," it said.
At the end of the current financial year all states except New South Wales and the Northern Territory will still have substantial excess supply of homes, Mellor said.
However, this surplus was being reduced, quite rapidly in some states and was expected to be halved by June 1998.
Mellor noted that new dwelling commencements fell 27 percent in 1995/96, the largest annual percentage decline for 21 years.
Commencements were expectted to fall again in the current year, but by only one percent, he said.
BIS Shrapnel's state by state outlook:

NEW SOUTH WALES: After almost four years to continuous growth, commencements fell 23 percent in 1995/96. The position improved in the December 1996 quarter with a 14 percent increase over the same period in 1995. The forecast for 1996/97 is for dwelling commencements to remain steady. By June this year the state is expected to have a small stock deficiency and
commencements are forecast to strengthen 12 percent in 1997/98.

VICTORIA: Dwelling commencements fell by nearly 30 percent between 1994 and 1996. A small decline is forecast for 1996/97 (two percent) and the market is then expected to embark on a weak recovery, strengthening towards the end of 1997. Victoria is expected to have a stock shortage of around 6,000 dwellings by June 1997 and, with underlying demand expected to increase over the next two years, this shortage will be exacerbated. This pent-up demand will drive a sharp recovery in 1997/98 (12 percent) and beyond.

QUEENSLAND: Commencements fell by one-third in 1995/96 following a 13 percent decline the previous year. The market began to recover in the December quarter 1996 largely as a result of a strong improvement in total other dwellings (36 percent). Growth is forecast to continue during the remainder of the financial year and to accelerate in 1998. The stock surplus was severe, but this oversupply is falling rapidly and 14 percent growth in commencements is forecast for 1997/98.

SOUTH AUSTRALIA: Commencements have been in almost continuous decline for the past three years and have more than halved since the last peak in 1993/94. Recovery is expected to have begun in the March quarter 1997 led by the private housing sector but growth is not expected to accelerate until the second half of 1997. The over-supply is still quite substantial. Forecasts are for a steady recovery of 13 percent to 6,150 in 1997/98 assisted by the state government's subsidy to first home buyers purchasing new homes. This incentive is likely to bring forward demand during 1997 to a level which may not be sustainable, and beyond 1998 low population growth will keep the
residential market relatively weak.

WESTERN AUSTRALIA: The downturn has been severe and affected all sectors. The oversupply of dwellings is still substantial, but may have been over-stated. BIS Shrapnel forecasts a 14 percent increase in commencements in 1997/98.

TASMANIA: Commencements fell by 20 percent in calendar 1996 to their lowest level since the 1950s. Construction was averaging 80 percent above underlying demand for the five years to 1994/95. The declines in construction levels, however, will bring back commencements to a level more in line with underlying demand. Activity will remain steady in 1997/98.

NORTHERN TERRITORY: The downturn was less severe than in other states and territories. The market is largely in balance with a small stock deficiency expected by the end of June. Commencements are expected to increase by eight percenT in 1997/98, a level which remains below underlying demand.

AUSTRALIAN CAPITAL TERRITORY: The downturn resulted in the lowest level of commencements in more than a decade with the private sector experiencing the most severe declines. A significant surplus of stock still exists. Commencements are expected to improve eight percent in 1997/98 to a level which remains below underlying demand, enabling the stock to be further reduced.
